ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_question_text: An NTC thermistor is a negative temperature coefficient thermistor, that is, it refers to a resistor whose resistance decreases as the temperature rises. The negative temperature coefficient thermistor R2 is connected into the circuit shown in the figure, R1 is a fixed resistor, and L is a small light bulb. When the temperature decreases (not considering the resistance of the bulb and the fixed resistor changing with temperature), how does the brightness of the small light bulb L change?
ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: The small light bulb becomes brighter
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: on the left side of the figure are the power supply and the ammeter, and above the circuit there is a fixed resistor R1; after passing through R1, it reaches a node, and from this node downward there are two branches: the middle branch is the small light bulb L, and the right branch is the thermistor R2; the lower ends of these two branches are again connected to the same bottom node. Therefore, the structure shown in the figure can be regarded as R1 in series with “the parallel combination of the small light bulb L and R2.” Then reason: the resistance of an NTC thermistor decreases as the temperature rises, so when the temperature decreases, the resistance of R2 increases. The equivalent resistance of the parallel part of L and R2 will increase as R2 increases; when this parallel part and R1 divide voltage in series, the voltage across the parallel part increases. The bulb L is in parallel with R2, so the voltage across the bulb L also increases. The problem states that the resistance of the bulb changing with temperature is not considered, so the bulb power P=U^2/R increases, and the brightness increases.
